li.a: Encyclopedia of Arkansas: Elaine Massacre of 1919
UA Little Rock exhibit: Overview of the Elaine Race Massacre
UA Little Rock exhibit: Moore v. Dempsey, with justice deferred the NAACP took action
Facing South: Arkansas' Phillips County remembers the racial massacre America forgot
Dark American History: The Elaine Massacre, Arkansas's Forgotten Bloodbath
Jacobin: The 1919 Elaine Massacre Was a Violent Response to Black Sharecropper Organizing
Mississippi Today: 1923, Supreme Court rules in Moore v. Dempsey

content.p: In the last days of September 1919, Black sharecroppers gathered in a church at Hoop Spur, in the cotton country of eastern Arkansas, to organise for fairer payment from the planters who owned the land. Within hours a shooting outside the church had turned into a manhunt across Phillips County. White posses, some of them deputised, killed an unknown number of Black residents, and historians cited below say soldiers sent by the governor took part. The Encyclopedia of Arkansas calls it by far the deadliest racial confrontation in the state's history and possibly the bloodiest in the nation's.

The number of Black dead has never been fixed. Historians cited by Facing South put it conservatively at 200, some contemporary counts run above 800, and Dark American History gives a range of 100 to 856. Five white people died. In the aftermath it was Black men who were put on trial: 122 were indicted and twelve were sentenced to death. No one who took part in the killing of Black residents was ever charged. The case of the condemned men eventually reached the United States Supreme Court and produced a ruling the UA Little Rock exhibit calls a landmark.

Sharecroppers in the Delta generally received payment once a year, at harvest. After paying for housing, land rent and goods bought at the plantation store, most broke even or stayed in debt, Jacobin notes. Accounts were kept by the planter and audited by no one, according to Dark American History, and a tenant who complained risked eviction or violence.

Cotton prices changed the arithmetic. Jacobin reports that cotton that had sold for around 14 cents a pound was fetching more than three times that in 1919, and landowners were making record profits. The Progressive Farmers and Household Union of America, which Jacobin says a Black man named Robert L. Hill had founded a year earlier, decided the moment had come. The UA Little Rock exhibit describes its aim: by pooling their money, members could pay lawyers to sue planters over stolen wages and false accounting. At Ratio, south of Elaine, members hired a white lawyer, Ulysses S. Bratton, to bring a suit.

The setting was tense. The Encyclopedia of Arkansas places the events in a year of racial conflict in Washington, Chicago, Knoxville and Indianapolis, with fear of labor unions and of Bolshevism running high after the First World War and Black soldiers returning home. Black residents outnumbered whites in this part of Phillips County by about ten to one, it says.

The union was noticed quickly. The UA Little Rock exhibit says that so-called "good negroes" told plantation owners about it soon after the Elaine chapter formed. Facing South describes white elites meeting at the old Opera House in Helena and deciding to break the union up by force. That account comes from the journalist's own summary of local history, and the sources opened here do not agree on how organised the white planning was.

On Tuesday 30 September roughly 100 people, mostly sharecroppers, attended a union meeting at the church. Union leaders had posted armed guards outside, the Encyclopedia of Arkansas says, to keep out disruption and white informers.

Accounts of what happened next conflict. The Encyclopedia of Arkansas and the UA Little Rock exhibit agree on the outcome: the dead man was W. A. Adkins, who worked as security officer for the Missouri Pacific Railroad, and the wounded man was Charles W. Pratt, the county's deputy sheriff; both were white. Both sources say the versions of who fired first are in sharp conflict. The officers' own story, according to the exhibit, was that they stopped at the church because of car trouble. A trustee from the Helena jail, "Kidd" Collins, was with them and escaped unhurt to Elaine, where he reported the shooting.

Jacobin tells it differently. Its account has three carloads of white men arriving around 11 p.m. and firing into the building, with the guards shooting back. It cites the journalist Ida B. Wells as estimating that eighty Black people died that night, and says the church and the bodies in it were burned afterwards. Dark American History says only that shooting broke out as law officers arrived. The reader is left with two accounts of the first shots and no neutral witness.

The telegraph carried the news. The UA Little Rock exhibit says that hundreds of white men came flooding in within hours, believing a Black revolt had to be put down. The Encyclopedia of Arkansas estimates that 500 to 1,000 armed white people, mostly from nearby Arkansas counties but also from across the river in Mississippi, travelled to Elaine. Jacobin says the sheriff deputised a posse of 300 by morning, including American Legion members, many of them First World War veterans.

On 1 October the county authorities sent three telegrams asking Governor Brough for federal troops. He obtained permission from the Department of War, and more than 500 soldiers from Camp Pike, outside Little Rock, were sent. Dark American History names the 583rd Engineers under Colonel Isaac Jenks and gives their orders as to "suppress the negro insurrection". The Encyclopedia of Arkansas says the troops reached Elaine on the morning of 2 October and that the white mobs then began to go home.

What the soldiers did is disputed. Jacobin says they carried rifles and machine guns and were told to shoot anyone who resisted being rounded up. The Encyclopedia of Arkansas says Colonel Jenks recorded only two Black people killed by the troops, whereas a Memphis Press correspondent wrote on 2 October that "Many Negroes are reported killed by the soldiers". It also cites Sharpe Dunaway, an employee of the Arkansas Gazette,, who alleged in a 1925 book that soldiers "committed one murder after another". The encyclopedia calls the claim that the military took part in the killing the more controversial one, and says anecdotal evidence points to it. Facing South says historians believe federal troops took part in the killing.

Black residents had few places to turn. The UA Little Rock exhibit says many hid in swamps and thickets, others were said to have been shot down while working in fields, and many surrendered. Soldiers held hundreds in makeshift stockades until their union ties were checked. Those who were not union members were held until landlords came to vouch for them, and the freed were handed passes and sent back to work. Jacobin adds that some prisoners were held in freight cars and one-room schoolhouses, and that in many cases the crops and belongings of those held were harvested, sold or removed.

Not every victim was in the union. The Encyclopedia of Arkansas names four Johnston brothers (David Augustine Elihue, Gibson Allen, Lewis Harrison and Leroy), attacked and killed on 2 October as they came back to Helena after hunting. Jacobin says that Ida B. Wells named the killer as Amos Jarman, the Helena postmaster and a county commissioner. That is her accusation as the article reports it; none of the pages opened shows that anyone was charged.

A local group called the Committee of Seven asked Governor Brough for authority to run the investigation and issue press updates, Jacobin says; it consisted of the sheriff, his acting sheriff, a judge, the Helena mayor and businessmen. The Encyclopedia of Arkansas says Brough accepted its authority in return for its promise that there would be no lynchings in Helena, and then told a press conference in Little Rock that the situation had been "well handled".

The Committee's version has an insurrection. On 7 October E. M. Allen, a planter and real estate developer who spoke for the white leadership, told the Helena World that the trouble was "not a race riot" but "a deliberately planned insurrection of the Negroes against the whites" directed by the union. Jacobin reports that a newspaper headline of the days that followed said Black people planned to kill all whites, and adds that, in its telling, no attack on white landowners or their families had taken place.

The NAACP challenged this from the start. It sent field secretary Walter White, who wrote in the Chicago Daily News on 19 October that the belief in an insurrection was "only a figment of the imagination of Arkansas whites and not based on fact". He added that white men in Helena had told him more than 100 Black people were killed. Ida B. Wells-Barnett secretly interviewed prisoners in Helena and wrote a pamphlet, The Arkansas Race Riot, which also rejected the insurrection claim and recorded torture of the prisoners.

Within days of the shooting, 285 Black men and women were taken from the stockades to the Helena jail, which had space for forty-eight, the Encyclopedia of Arkansas says. In sworn affidavits in 1921 two white posse members, T. K. Jones and H. F. Smiddy, said they had committed acts of torture at the jail and named others who had done the same. The UA Little Rock exhibit says the 1921 affidavits claimed that prisoners had been tortured into testifying against one another.

On 31 October 1919 the Phillips County grand jury charged 122 Black people, with offences from murder to nightriding. The trials began the following week. Circuit Judge J. M. Jackson appointed white Helena lawyers to represent the first twelve defendants. One of them, Jacob Fink, admitted to the jury that he had spoken to no witnesses, the Encyclopedia says; he asked for no change of venue and challenged no juror, accepting the first twelve called. By 5 November the twelve had been convicted of murder and sentenced to the electric chair. Dark American History says each trial lasted forty-five minutes or less, the juries were all white, no defence witnesses were called and the verdicts came within minutes. Sixty-five other defendants then accepted plea bargains with sentences of up to twenty-one years for second-degree murder, according to the Encyclopedia of Arkansas; Dark American History says sixty-seven received prison sentences.
The Encyclopedia of Arkansas lists the men later called the Elaine Twelve as Moore, the brothers Frank and Ed Hicks, Knox, Hall, Coleman, Banks, Ware, Wordlaw, Giles, Fox and Martin.
content.h2: Scipio Jones and the fight to Washington
content.p: Scipio Africanus Jones, the leading Black lawyer in Arkansas of his time, began raising money for the defence in Little Rock. On the advice of Ulysses Bratton, the NAACP in New York retained the Little Rock firm of George Murphy, a former Confederate officer and state attorney general, then seventy-nine. By late November Jones was working alongside it, according to the Encyclopedia of Arkansas.

The cases split in two. Six men, the Ware defendants, won new trials because the trial judge had not required jurors to state the degree of murder on their ballots. Jones led the retrials, which began on 3 May 1920. Local white hostility toward him was so intense, the encyclopedia says, that he reportedly spent each night of the trials under a different Black family's roof, afraid for his life. The convictions were affirmed again but the Arkansas Supreme Court ended up freeing the men after two terms of court passed without the state moving to retry them.

The other six, the Moore defendants, lost their appeal when the Arkansas Supreme Court upheld their verdicts on 29 March 1920. Their position looked bleak, in the UA Little Rock exhibit's words, until the summer of 1921, when two affidavits from white witnesses reached Jones alleging that prisoners had been tortured into testifying. He took the case to federal court. The state's attorney general responded only with a demurrer, in effect saying the facts alleged were irrelevant even if true, and Judge J. H. Cotteral denied a federal trial. The NAACP appealed again.

On 19 February 1923 the US Supreme Court ruled 6 to 2 in Moore v. Dempsey in the defendants' favour. The exhibit says the justices held that the trials had been dominated by a mob, quoting the finding that the corrective process available "does not seem sufficient", and that federal judges could therefore overturn state criminal verdicts to protect due process. Dark American History stresses that the ruling did not find the men innocent; it found the trials a fraud. The Encyclopedia of Arkansas adds that the court regarded the Helena proceedings as a "mask".

The ruling did not free the Moore men immediately. The exhibit says they faced a possible retrial, and that Jones moved to avoid more trials and secure release. On 3 November 1923 Governor Thomas McRae commuted the death sentences to twelve years, making them eligible for parole. The Encyclopedia of Arkansas describes it differently: Jones negotiated in March 1923 for the men to plead guilty to second-degree murder, and on 13 January 1925 McRae ordered their release by indefinite furlough. Both sources agree the six were freed on that date.

Robert Hill had meanwhile escaped. The Encyclopedia of Arkansas says friends hid him and he later fled to Kansas. Dark American History says he was arrested there, extradited and then released. Facing South quotes the historian Brian Mitchell as saying two hundred people followed Hill with nothing but the shirts they wore, and says many Black families left Phillips County after the killings.

For decades the white version of events held. Dark American History blames the rural setting, the persistence of the "negro insurrection" label, and the fact that no one who took part in the killing was ever charged. The encyclopedia says that some local white residents still argue the mobs acted properly to forestall a slaughter, while the view of most historians today is that white mobs unjustifiably killed an undetermined number of Black people. A 2000 conference in Helena brought no closure, it adds. A documentary, The Elaine Massacre: Tragedy and Triumph, funded by the Winthrop Rockefeller Foundation, went to every Arkansas school district in 2002.

Facing South says the massacre has never been part of the state's classroom curriculum, and that historians including Mitchell have built an online exhibit and curriculum guide. It credits the Moore decision with widening the Supreme Court's power to review state criminal cases, and notes that some Progressive Farmers members later joined the Southern Tenant Farmers Union, formed in Tyronza, Arkansas, in 1934.

The centenary, in September 2019, was a divided occasion. A memorial was dedicated in Helena-West Helena on 29 September, the Encyclopedia of Arkansas records, and the Elaine Twelve were honoured on the Arkansas Civil Rights Heritage Trail in Little Rock on 5 November. In Elaine the Elaine Legacy Center held its own commemoration. Facing South reports that many Elaine residents were unhappy that the memorial stood in Helena, which they felt would bring tourism money to the town where the posses formed and the trials were held. Federal judge Brian Miller, whose four great-uncles were among those killed, was among the leaders of the Helena memorial committee. Circuit Judge Wendell Griffen said it showed the city profiting from the county's trauma. The centre's tour took visitors to the former church site and to two mass graves, one inside Elaine and one at Lakeview; a willow planted near the Elaine grave earlier in 2019 was cut down within months, which those who planted it believe was a hate crime.

The same Facing South report describes present-day Elaine. 65 percent of Black residents lived below the poverty line, compared with 13 percent of white residents, and the population had shrunk to about 500. At the centennial events Facing South heard residents call for reparations and for the return of land, and a litany read at a church service spoke of a debt left unpaid for 100 years.
